title: The camel and the eye of the needle
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα τὴν κατὰ τῶν πλουσίων ἀπόφασιν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, εἰπόντος· „εὐκοπώτερον κάμηλον εἰσελθεῖν διὰ τρήματος ῥαφίδος ἢ πλούσιον εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ,“ φησὶν ἄντικρυς ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι, τοῦ Ἰησοῦ παραφθείροντος τὸ Πλατωνικὸν, ἐν οἷς εἶπεν ὁ Πλάτων ὅτι „ἀγαθὸν ὄντα διαφόρως καὶ πλούσιον εἶναι διαφερόντως εἶναι ἀδύνατον.“ τίς δ᾿ οὐκ ἂν καὶ μετρίως ἐφιστάνειν τοῖς πράγμασι δυνάμενος τὸν Κέλσον γελάσαι, οὐ τῶν πιστευόντων τῷ Ἰησοῦ μόνων ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἀκούων ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ὁ παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις γεγενημένος καὶ ἀνατεθραμμένος καὶ Ἰωσὴφ „τοῦ τέκτονος“ νομισθεὶς εἶναι υἱὸς καὶ μηδὲ γράμματα μεμαθηκὼς οὐ μόνον τὰ Ἑλλήνων ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ τὰ Ἑβραίων, ὅπερ καὶ αἱ φιλαλήθεις μαρτυροῦσι γραφαὶ τῶν περὶ αὐτὸν, ἀνέγνω Πλάτωνα καὶ ἀρεσθεὶς τῇ περὶ τῶν πλουσίων ἀποφαινομένῃ αὐτοῦ λέξει, ὡς „ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν ἀγαθὸν εἶναι διαφερόντως καὶ πλούσιον,“ παρέφθειρεν αὐτὴν καὶ πεποίηκε τὸ „εὐκοπώτερον κάμηλον διὰ τρήματος ῥαφίδος εἰσελθεῖν ἢ πλούσιον εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ“; εἰ δὲ μὴ μετὰ τοῦ μισεῖν καὶ ἀπεχθάνεσθαι ἐντυχὼν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις φιλαλήθης ἦν ὁ Κέλσος, ἐπέστησεν ἂν, τί δή ποτε παρελήφθη κάμηλος, τὸ τῶν ζῴων ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ κατασκευῇ σκολιὸν, παραβαλλόμενον τῷ πλουσίῳ, καὶ τί αὐτῷ ἐβούλετο ἡ στενὴ „τῆς ῥαφίδος“ τρυμαλιὰ, στενὴν φάσκοντι εἶναι καὶ τεθλιμμένην τὴν ὁδὸν τὴν ἀπάγουσαν „εἰς τὴν ζωὴν,“ καὶ τὸ κατὰ τὸν νόμον δὲ „ἀκάθαρτον“ τὸ ζῷον ἀναγεγράφθαι τοῦτο, ἔχον μέν τι ἀποδεκτὸν τὸ μαρυκᾶσθαι, ἔχον δὲ καὶ ψεκτὸν τὸ μὴ διχηλεῖν· ἐξήτασεν ἂν καὶ ὁσάκις ἐν ταῖς θείαις παρελήφθη κάμηλος γραφαῖς καὶ ἐπὶ τίνων, ἵνα θεωρήσῃ τὸ περὶ τῶν πλουσίων τοῦ λόγου βούλημα· οὐκ εἴασεν ἂν ἀβασάνιστον καὶ τὸ μακαρίζεσθαι μὲν τοὺς πτωχοὺς ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ταλανίζεσθαι δὲ τοὺς πλουσίους πότερον ἐπὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν αὐτῷ ταῦτα . . . . πτωχῶν καὶ πλουσίων, ἢ οἶδέ τινα πτωχείαν πάντως μακαριζομένην ὁ λόγος καὶ πλοῦτον πάντως ψεκτόν· οὐκ ἂν γὰρ οὐδ᾿ ὁ τυχὼν ἀκρίτως τοὺς πτωχοὺς ἐπῄνεσεν, ὧν οἱ πολλοὶ καὶ φαυλόττοί εἰσι τὰ ἤθη. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ταύτῃ.
pass_a_gloss: After these, the pronouncement (ἀπόφασις) of Jesus against the rich (πλούσιοι), [he] saying: 'easier (εὐκοπώτερον) a camel (κάμηλος) to enter through a hole (τρῆμα) of a needle (ῥαφίς) than a rich man into the kingdom (βασιλεία) of God,' he says was said outright (ἄντικρυς) from Plato, Jesus corrupting (παραφθείροντος) the Platonic [saying], in which Plato said that 'being good exceptionally and being rich exceptionally (διαφερόντως) is impossible (ἀδύνατον).' Who, able even moderately (μετρίως) to attend (ἐφιστάνειν) to the facts (πράγματα), would not laugh at Celsus, not only of those believing in Jesus but also of the rest of men, hearing that Jesus, born and brought up among Jews, and supposed (νομισθείς) to be son of Joseph 'the carpenter (τέκτων)', and not having learned letters (γράμματα), not only those of the Greeks but not even those of the Hebrews, which the truth-loving (φιλαλήθεις) writings (γραφαί) of those about him also testify (μαρτυροῦσι), read Plato and, pleased (ἀρεσθείς) with his saying (λέξις) declaring about the rich that 'it is impossible to be exceptionally good and rich', corrupted it and made 'easier a camel through a hole of a needle to enter than a rich man into the kingdom of God'? But if, not reading (ἐντυχών) the gospels with hating and hostility (ἀπεχθάνεσθαι), Celsus had been truth-loving, he would have considered (ἐπέστησεν) why ever a camel was taken (παρελήφθη), the animal crooked (σκολιόν) as far as its structure (κατασκευή), compared (παραβαλλόμενον) with the rich man, and what the narrow opening (τρυμαλιά) 'of the needle' meant (ἐβούλετο) to him who says (φάσκοντι) narrow and pressed/hard (τεθλιμμένην) is the way leading away 'into life', and that according to the law (νόμος) this animal has been recorded (ἀναγεγράφθαι) 'unclean (ἀκάθαρτον)', having something acceptable (ἀποδεκτόν), the chewing the cud (μαρυκᾶσθαι), but having also something blameworthy (ψεκτόν), the not dividing the hoof (διχηλεῖν); he would have examined (ἐξήτασεν) also how often in the divine Scriptures (θεῖαι γραφαί) the camel was taken up and in connection with whom (ἐπὶ τίνων), so that he might contemplate (θεωρήσῃ) the intent (βούλημα) of the word (λόγος) about the rich; he would not have left untested (ἀβασάνιστον) also the poor being called blessed (μακαρίζεσθαι) by Jesus and the rich being called wretched (ταλανίζεσθαι), whether these [were said] by him about the sense-perceptible (αἰσθητοί) [lacuna] poor and rich, or the word knows (οἶδε) some poverty (πτωχεία) blessed in every way (πάντως) and wealth (πλοῦτος) blameworthy in every way; for not even the ordinary person would undiscriminatingly (ἀκρίτως) have praised the poor, of whom the many are also most worthless (φαυλότατοι) in characters (ἤθη). But these things thus.
pass_b_english: After this he takes the pronouncement of Jesus against the rich, when he said, “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24), and says that it was plainly borrowed from Plato, and that Jesus corrupted Plato’s saying where Plato said that “for one who is exceptionally good to be exceptionally rich as well is impossible” (Plato, Laws 5.742e–743a).

Who with even a moderate power to weigh the facts, not only among those who believe in Jesus but among the rest of mankind as well, would not laugh at Celsus on hearing that Jesus, who was born and brought up among the Jews, who was thought to be the son of Joseph “the carpenter” (Luke 3:23; Matthew 13:55), and who had not learned letters, not only those of the Greeks but not even those of the Hebrews (John 7:15), as the truth-loving writings about him also testify, read Plato, and, pleased with his saying about the rich, that “it is impossible to be exceptionally good and rich,” corrupted it and turned it into “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24)?

If Celsus had loved the truth, and had not read the Gospels with hatred and hostility, he would have considered why a camel was chosen for comparison with the rich man, an animal crooked in its build; and what Jesus meant by the narrow “eye of the needle” (Mark 10:25), since he says that the way that leads “to life” is narrow and hard (Matthew 7:14); and the fact that in the law this animal is recorded as “unclean,” having something acceptable, in that it chews the cud, but also something to be blamed, in that it does not part the hoof (Leviticus 11:4; Deuteronomy 14:7). He would also have examined how often the camel is mentioned in the divine Scriptures, and in connection with whom, so as to see the intent of the saying about the rich. Nor would he have left unexamined the fact that Jesus calls the poor blessed and the rich wretched (Luke 6:20, 24): whether these words of his […] refer to the poor and the rich as the senses perceive them, or whether the Word knows a poverty that is wholly blessed and a wealth that is wholly to be blamed. For not even an ordinary person would praise the poor without discrimination, since most of them are of very bad character. But enough of this.

choices.choice: Lacuna: Koetschau marks a gap after αὐτῷ ταῦτα; a verb such as εἴρηται (‘were said’) is probably lost. The English marks [lacuna] and supplies ‘refer to’ only to make the clause readable; nothing else is supplied. The camel saying in Origen’s wording (τρήματος ῥαφίδος εἰσελθεῖν) is closest to Matthew 19:24 (parallels Mark 10:25, Luke 18:25); the later phrase ‘the narrow eye (τρυμαλιά) of the needle’ uses Mark’s word (Mark 10:25). The Plato sentence (Laws 5.742e–743a; the range is given because the sentence falls at the page turn) is garbled in the copy-text (διαφόρως... εἶναι διαφερόντως εἶναι); translated in the sense of Plato’s text and of Origen’s own repetition later in the chapter. Celsus’s claim that the saying was ‘plainly borrowed from Plato’ and ‘corrupted’ is indirect speech in the Greek and is kept without quotation marks. ‘Thought to be the son of Joseph’ echoes Luke 3:23 (ὡς ἐνομίζετο) and ‘the carpenter’ Matthew 13:55 (‘the carpenter’s son’); ‘had not learned letters’ echoes John 7:15. τῶν περὶ αὐτόν may mean ‘of those around him’ (his disciples) or simply ‘about him’; rendered ‘about him’. The camel as unclean: Leviticus 11:4 and Deuteronomy 14:7. ‘Called... wretched’ (ταλανίζεσθαι) refers to the woes on the rich in Luke 6:24, with the blessing of the poor in Luke 6:20. ὁ λόγος in ‘the Word knows a poverty’ is rendered ‘the Word’; it may mean the scriptural teaching rather than Christ the Word. φαυλόττοί in the staged text is a typo for φαυλότατοι.
